overall_summary: Space and extreme exoplanet topics are the clear growth drivers for FACTVERSE, with concepts focusing on bizarre planetary weather (raining rubies, glass, or molten iron), extreme physics (burning ice, coal-dark planets), and high-value hypothetical scenarios ($26 nonillion diamond planet) generating the highest views and engagement. Conversely, general psychology facts and basic animal trivia consistently underperform, indicating the audience prefers mind-bending cosmic mysteries over everyday science.

winning_patterns.evidence: 'The Planet of Burning Ice' (1,055 views), 'The Planet Darker Than Coal' (1,025 views), and 'This Planet Rains Supersonic Rubies!' (721 views) are the top-performing videos.
winning_patterns.action: Double down on exoplanets with extreme, visually dramatic environmental conditions. Focus on sensory-rich descriptions like 'raining gems', 'screaming winds', or 'burning ice'.

winning_patterns.evidence: 'What If You Fell Into This $26 Nonillion Diamond Planet?' (487 views) and 'What If You Visited the Sunscreen Planet?' (337 views) show strong viewer interest when abstract space facts are framed as personal, high-stakes journeys.
winning_patterns.action: Frame future space facts as immersive first-person hypothetical scenarios to boost viewer retention and emotional investment.

weak_patterns.evidence: 'Your Brain Can Create Fake Memories' (max 53 views across multiple uploads) and 'The Real Reason Songs Get Stuck In Your Head' (17 views) failed to capture audience interest.
weak_patterns.action: Pause production on general psychology and cognitive bias content, or strictly reframe them through a high-stakes survival or horror/mystery lens.

weak_patterns.evidence: 'Octopuses Have THREE Hearts' (12s, 183 views) and 'The Only Animal That Can Live Forever' (16s, 69 views) underperform compared to cosmic topics.
weak_patterns.action: Avoid common, easily searchable animal facts. If covering biology, pivot to cinematic animal survival narratives or bizarre evolutionary anomalies with longer, story-driven structures.

next_video.concept: What If You Fell Into Gliese 436b (The Planet of Burning Ice)?
next_video.opening_direction: Imagine stepping onto a planet where the ice is literally on fire at 800 degrees Fahrenheit, but it never melts.
next_video.twist_direction: The gravity is so incredibly intense that it forces water molecules to stay packed into a solid state, creating a scorching, gravity-defying paradox.
next_video.reason: Gliese 436b ('burning ice') was the channel's top-performing concept (1,055 views). Transforming this proven topic into a high-retention 'What If' format—which also succeeded with the diamond planet—maximizes the probability of viral performance.
